chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhl narrated from Mu'awiya ibn Hakim and Ya'qub al-Katib, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Zayd al-Narsi, from Ali ibn Mazyad, the companion of al-Sabiri, who said:

A man bequeathed his estate to me and ordered me to perform Hajj on his behalf with it. I looked into the matter and found it to be a small amount that would not suffice for Hajj. So I asked Abu Hanifa and the jurists of Ahl al-Kufa, and they said: 'Give it in charity on his behalf.' When I had performed Hajj, I came to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and said: 'May I be your ransom, a man died and bequeathed his estate to me to perform Hajj on his behalf. I looked into it and it did not suffice for Hajj, so I asked the jurists among us and they said: 'Give it in charity.' He asked: 'What did you do?' I said: 'I gave it in charity.' He said: 'Did you guarantee, or will it not suffice to perform Hajj with it from Mecca? If it does not suffice to perform Hajj with it from Mecca, then there is no guarantee upon you. But if it suffices to perform Hajj with it from Mecca, then you are liable (guarantor).'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if an estate is too small to perform Hajj but the executor gives it in charity instead?
ai.summary: This hadith highlights the jurisprudential divergence between the Kufan jurists, who advised charity for insufficient funds, and Imam al-Sadiq (AS), who introduced a precise condition based on the sufficiency of the amount to perform Hajj from Mecca. The Imam’s ruling establishes that if the funds are sufficient to complete the pilgrimage, the executor remains liable (daman) for fulfilling the obligation, whereas insufficient funds exempt him from guarantee upon charitable distribution. This distinction underscores the Shia emphasis on the actual capacity to fulfill the religious duty rather than merely disposing of the estate.
